=== Morphological Assessment Form ===
A. Leaf Arrangement & Architecture
    1. Leaf relative position (alternate / opposite / whorled): alternate (leaves attach at successive nodes along the stem, alternating sides; no paired or whorled nodes visible)
    2. Leaf spacing (clustered / distal): distal (leaves are spaced along the stem with visible internodes, not clustered at the apex)

B. Leaf Complexity
    3. Leaf complexity (simple / compound): compound (each leaf has multiple leaflets attached to a central rachis)
    4. Compound leaf type, ONLY if leaf complexity is compound (odd-pinnate / even-pinnate): odd-pinnate (terminal leaflet present at the end of the rachis; lateral leaflets paired along the rachis)
    5. Number of leaflets (integer estimate 2, 4, 8, …): 8 (based on visible compound leaves; each leaf has approximately 4 pairs of lateral leaflets plus a terminal leaflet, totaling 9; however, due to partial views and damage, 8 is the best estimate for consistent count across images)
    6. Leaflet arrangement (opposite / alternate / subopposite): opposite (leaflets are arranged in pairs along the rachis, with each pair at a node)

C. Leaf Morphology
    7. Leaf margin (entire / toothed) AND if toothed (dentate, serrate, etc.)): toothed, serrate (margins have small, sharp teeth pointing forward along the margin, consistent with serration)
    8. Leaf shape (elliptic, obovate, lanceolate, etc.): lanceolate (leaflets are elongated with a broad base tapering to a pointed apex)
    9. Leaf apex (acute, obtuse, acuminate): acute (apex is sharply pointed but not drawn out into a long tip)
    10. Leaf base (rounded, cordate, cuneate): cuneate (base is wedge-shaped, tapering to the petiolule)
    11. Venation type (pinnate / palmate / parallel): pinnate (main vein runs from base to apex, with secondary veins branching off and curving toward margin)
    12. Secondary veins (visibility, spacing, number): visible, closely spaced, numerous (secondary veins are clearly visible, running parallel to each other and curving toward the margin; many per leaflet)
    13. Leaf surface features (glabrous, shiny, dull, rugose): dull, glabrous (surface is not shiny, appears matte; no visible hairs)
    14. Leaf surface trichomes (present / absent): absent (no visible trichomes or hairs on leaf surface)
    15. Petiole length (short / long): short (petiole is short, supporting the compound leaf; rachis is elongated)
    16. Petiole features (winged / grooved / terete): terete (petiole is round in cross-section, no wings or grooves visible)

D. Stem & Shoot Traits
    17. Stem type, may not be visible (woody / herbaceous): herbaceous (stem appears green and soft, not woody; typical of seedling stage)
    18. Stem trichomes (present / absent): absent (no visible trichomes on stem)
    19. Stem color: green (stem is green, consistent with young growth)
    20. Stem texture (smooth / ridged / lenticellate): smooth (stem surface is smooth without ridges or lenticels)

E. Other Visible Seedling Traits
    21. Stipules, sometimes visible only in close-up images (present / absent): absent (no stipules visible at leaf bases)
    22. Latex, rarely visible but extremely diagnostic when present (present / not observed): not observed (no latex exudate visible)
    23. Pulvinus, for Fabaceae family only (present / absent): absent (no pulvinus visible at leaflet or leaf bases; not applicable for Fabaceae due to lack of diagnostic features, but noted as absent)
    24. Tendrils (present / absent): absent (no tendrils observed)

F. Notes: Several leaflets show damage with holes and margin irregularities, likely from physical or biological causes; some leaflets appear partially eaten or abraded. Multiple views confirm compound, odd-pinnate leaf structure with serrate margins and alternate leaf arrangement. Petiole is short and terete; rachis is elongated. No stipules, latex, or tendrils observed. Stem is herbaceous and green. All observations are based on visible features without inference of species or family.

rag_matches.description: Tree, to 8 m tall; branchlets, petioles, rachises, leaflets, below, and midribs above densely short-pubescent; lenticels ± prominent, small. Petiole and rachis not winged; leaflets in 4-8 pairs, variable in shape, asymmetrical, mostly narrowly ovate to elliptic, acute to long-acuminate, obtuse to rounded at base, puberulent above except on midrib, the terminal pair 7-10(15) cm long, 2.5-4(6) cm wide. Spikes axillary or terminal, in groups of 1-4; peduncles 3-4 cm long, densely tomentose; bracts 1 mm long; calyx 3-5 mm long, the lobes acute, ca 0.5 mm long, tomentose; corolla 14-20 mm long, sericeous-villous, the lobes to 1.5 mm long. Legumes flat, 6-20 cm long, 1.5-2.5 cm wide, bearing dense short, ferruginous-tomentose pubescence, the marginal ribs prominent. Rare; collected along the shore of Gigante Bay and Burrunga Point. Seasonal behavior uncertain. Flowers from January to May. The fruits were mature in the rainy season. Confused with Inga multijuga, which often has nine or ten pairs of leaflets. Belize to Panama; Trinidad. In Panama, known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone and Darien and from tropical wet forest in Colon (Salud) and Darien.

Tree, to 15 m tall; branchlets sparsely strigose when young, glabrate in age, minutely lenticellate, minutely ribbed below petioles (at least when dried). Leaves strigose throughout, especially on axis and midrib of leaflets; petiole and rachis terete to narrowly margined; leaflets in 2 or 3 pairs, lanceolate to elliptic, long-acuminate, acute to rounded at base, the terminal pair 9-18 cm long, 3.5-7.5 cm wide. Spikes axillary, in groups of 1-7; peduncle and rachis strigose; peduncles 2-4 cm long; rachis much shorter, 1-2.5 cm long; bracts subulate, to ± 2 mm long; calyx puberulent, 3-5 mm long, the lobes ± 1 mm long; corolla moderately sericeous, 5-9 mm long, the lobes to 2 mm long; stamens and style to ca 2 cm long. Legumes flat, to 16 cm long and 2 cm wide, minutely puberulent, the margins raised. Common in the forest. Flowers throughout the rainy season (May to December, rarely to January). One individual Inga punctata on Barro Colorado Island flowered for a week in early June in two consecutive years. Mature fruits seen in late dry season. Fruits are similar to those of Inga pezizifera, but that species lacks persistent warty fruit bases. Mexico to Peru; West Indies. In Panama, known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Bocas del Toro, San Bias, Veraguas, Panama, and Darien, from premontane wet forest in Colon, Chiriqui, Code, and Panama, from tropical wet forest in Panama and Darien and from lower montane wet forest in Chiriqui.

Shrubby herb or shrub, 0.3-0.8 m; young twigs ferruginous-tomentose or ferruginous-pubescent with trichomes <0.2 mm to glabrescent. Leaves ± isomorphic; petiole 0.9-1.5 cm; blade 5.5-19 X 2.4-9.3 cm, elliptical to obovate-elliptical, cuneate at the base, acute to shortly acuminate at the tip, thin and irregularly pectinate-dentate, inconspicuously pubescent on the nerves (especially on the underside) to glabrescent, with inconspicuous punctations on the underside. Inflorescences terminal, erect, corymbose-paniculated, 2-4-pinnate, 2.8-15.2 cm, ferruginous-pubescent with trichomes <0.2 mm, the rachis usually straight, the flowers densely clustered, distributed in the distal half of the axes; peduncle absent or up to ca. 1.9 cm; bracts up to ca. 5 mm, scarious. Flowers with pedicel 4-6 mm; sepals 1.7-2.6 mm; petals purple, 2.2-3.8 mm; anthers 0.9-1.4 mm. Fruits 4-5 mm. Very wet forest, 0-900+ m; [in the vertical Caribbean Cordillera Central, in the eastern Cordillera de Talamanca (Amubri), in the Plains of Los Guatusos and San Carlos, in the Baja Talamanca, in the vertical Pacific Cordilleras de Guanacaste and Tilarán, in the northern Fila Costeña, in the protected area of Parque Nacional Carara]. Fl. Apr.-Jul. [in Mexico, Peru, and Venezuela].

Shrubby herb or shrub, 0.3-0.8 m; young twigs ferruginous-tomentose or ferruginous-pubescent with trichomes <0.2 mm to glabrescent. Leaves ± isomorphic; petiole 0.9-1.5 cm; blade 5.5-19 X 2.4-9.3 cm, elliptical to obovate-elliptical, cuneate at the base, acute to shortly acuminate at the tip, thin and irregularly pectinate-dentate, inconspicuously pubescent on the nerves (especially on the underside) to glabrescent, with inconspicuous punctations on the underside. Inflorescences terminal, erect, corymbose-paniculated, 2-4-pinnate, 2.8-15.2 cm, ferruginous-pubescent with trichomes <0.2 mm, the rachis usually straight, the flowers densely clustered, distributed in the distal half of the axes; peduncle absent or up to ca. 1.9 cm; bracts up to ca. 5 mm, scarious. Flowers with pedicel 4-6 mm; sepals 1.7-2.6 mm; petals purple, 2.2-3.8 mm; anthers 0.9-1.4 mm. Fruits 4-5 mm. Very wet forest, 0-900+ m; [in the vertical Caribbean Cordillera Central], [in the eastern Cordillera de Talamanca (Amubri)], [in the Plains of Los Guatusos and San Carlos], [in the Baja Talamanca], [in the vertical Pacific Cordilleras de Guanacaste and Tilarán], [in the northern Fila Costeña], [in the protected area of P.N. Carara]. Fl. Apr.-Jul. [in the regions of Mexico, Peru and Venezuela].

Tree, to 30 m tall and 40 cm dbh (often much shorter along the shore); outer bark hard, closely fissured; inner bark red; younger stems, leaf rachises, and axes of inflorescences densely strigose and puberulent (in Panama) or sparsely strigose, sparsely puberulent, or nearly glabrous (often in South America). Leaves alternate, imparipinnate, mostly 15-30 cm long; petioles flat on upper surface with marginal ribs; leaflets apparently never dimorphic, usually 5-9 (rarely 3 or 10), usually alternate, ± elliptic, acuminate, obtuse-attenuate at base, 4-21 cm long, 1.5-8 cm wide, usually glabrous or minutely puberulent and/or strigose on midrib on both surfaces, rarely strigose below; midrib sharply raised. Panicles axillary (often appearing terminal), mostly 8-20 cm long; flowers white or greenish-yellow, 4-6-parted, as wide as long, globular in bud, the trichomes (at least on calyx) erect or appressed; calyx saucer-shaped, the lobes acute or blunt; petals valvate, ovate, to ca 2 mm long, glabrous or sparsely appressed-pubescent outside, glabrous inside, the margins papillose-puberulent; staminal tube two-thirds to three-fourths as long as petals, broader than long, glabrous outside and in but sometimes pubescent inside near apex, the lobes narrowly acute; anthers twice as many as petals, very narrowly ovoid, ca 0.5 mm long, alternating with and usually longer than lobes of staminal tube; ovary broadly ovoid, densely appressed-pubescent with white trichomes all over; style usually glabrous. Capsules ellipsoid, 11-18 mm long, orange at maturity, prominently tuberculate, the 3 (4) valves folding back to expose shiny red aril; seeds 1 or 2, smooth, ellipsoid, ca 1 cm long. Abundant as seedlings; common as adults in the forest, especially in the old forest. Flowering is bimodal, but principally from April to June, especially in June; a second but much smaller flowering period may occur from September to November. [unclear reference] The fruits from the first flowering mature mostly during September and October, especially in October; mature fruits from the second flowering have been seen in June.

Guavita cansa-boca, Bribri, Guava, Guava del mono Tree, to 15 m tall; branchlets sparsely strigose when young, glabrate in age, minutely lenticellate, minutely ribbed below petioles (at least when dried). Leaves strigose throughout, especially on axis and midrib of leaflets; petiole and rachis terete to narrowly margined; leaflets in 2 or 3 pairs, lanceolate to elliptic, long-acuminate, acute to rounded at base, the terminal pair 9-18 cm long, 3.5-7.5 cm wide. Spikes axillary, in groups of 1-7; peduncle and rachis strigose; peduncles 2-4 cm long; rachis much shorter, 1-2.5 cm long; bracts subulate, to ± 2 mm long; calyx puberulent, 3-5 mm long, the lobes ± 1 mm long; corolla moderately sericeous, 5-9 mm long, the lobes to 2 mm long; stamens and style to ca 2 cm long. Legumes flat, to 16 cm long and 2 cm wide, minutely puberulent, the margins raised.

Tree, 5-20 m tall; outer bark minutely fissured, thin (bearing short, raised, horizontal lines on inner surface); inner bark reddish-brown on the outer edge, bearing impressed short horizontal lines, the sap with sweet, distinctive aroma; young twigs, rachises, axes of inflorescences and of leaves moderately short-appressed pubescent, glabrous in age. Leaves alternate, pinnate, mostly 8-25 cm long, essentially glabrous; petioles flat on upper surface with marginal ribs; leaflets usually alternate, often dimorphic, those of full size usually 3-5, often with 1 or 2 pairs of minute, aborted leaflets at base, rarely with 7 full-sized leaflets, the blades ± elliptic, acuminate, acute to obtuse at base, 6-16 cm long, 2.5-6(7) cm wide; major lateral veins mostly 8-12, scarcely raised below, joining before the margin, the midrib usually flat above. Panicles solitary in upper axils, 5-17 cm long; flowers greenish, mostly 5-parted; calyx bowl-shaped, shallowly lobed, 1-2 mm long, glabrate; petals ovate, 2-3 mm long, usually glabrous but with minute papillae on margin; staminal tube one-half to two-thirds as long as petals, much broader than long, moderately to sparsely pubescent outside at least toward base (often glabrous outside in South America), sparsely to densely pubescent inside; anthers twice the number of petals, slender, slightly tapered toward apex, ca 1 mm long, dehiscing along lateral margins, alternating with and ± equaling acicular lobes of staminal tube; ovary broadly ovoid, 1-2 mm wide, with 2 or 3 (4) locules, the trichomes dense, appressed, white on basal half; style ± equaling ovary at anthesis; stigma capitate, inconspicuously lobed, held about at height of anthers. Fruits ± globose, green at maturity, weakly verrucose, 2-3 cm diam, ± glabrous, dehiscing by 3 valves; seeds 1 or 2, covered with a shiny red aril. Rare; collected only along the shore between Bat Cove and the dock. Flowers from March to May. The fruits mature from August to September.

Tree, to 27 m tall and 40 cm dbh, glabrous to puberulent throughout; trunk ± involuted with many prominent horizontal wrinkles; outer bark thin; inner bark reddish; young stems very prominently lenticellate. Petioles margined; rachis margined to narrowly winged; leaflets in 2-5 (usually 4) pairs, narrowly ovate to lanceolate-elliptic or oblanceolate, acuminate, rounded to acute at base, slightly asymmetrical, the terminal pair 8-22 cm long, 2.5-8 cm wide. Spikes axillary in groups of 1-6; peduncles 1.5-3.5 cm long; rachis shorter than peduncle, very densely flowered, 0.5-3 cm long; bracts ca 5 mm long; flowers sessile; calyx 1-2(3) mm long, the lobes ca 0.5 mm long, blunt; corolla 4-8 mm long, the lobes blunt to acute, ca 1 mm long; stamens and style ca 1 cm long. Legumes flat, 10-22 cm long, (2)2.5-3 cm wide, ± glabrous, ± straight, the marginal ribs prominent, the fruits probably mature from July to October. Known only from Panama, from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Bocas del Toro, San Bias, Veraguas, Panama, and Darien, from premontane wet forest in Colon, Chiriqui, Code, and Panama.

Tree, to 27 m tall and 40 cm dbh, glabrous to puberulent throughout; trunk ± involuted with many prominent horizontal wrinkles; outer bark thin; inner bark reddish; young stems very prominently lenticellate. Petioles margined; rachis margined to narrowly winged; leaflets in 2-5 (usually 4) pairs, narrowly ovate to lanceolate-elliptic or oblanceolate, acuminate, rounded to acute at base, slightly asymmetrical, the terminal pair 8-22 cm long, 2.5-8 cm wide. Spikes axillary in groups of 1-6; peduncles 1.5-3.5 cm long; rachis shorter than peduncle, very densely flowered, 0.5-3 cm long; bracts ca 5 mm long; flowers sessile; calyx 1-2(3) mm long, the lobes ca 0.5 mm long, blunt; corolla 4-8 mm long, the lobes blunt to acute, ca 1 mm long; stamens and style ca 1 cm long. Legumes flat, 10-22 cm long, (2)2.5-3 cm wide, ± glabrous, ± straight, the marginal ribs prominent.

Tree, to 15 m tall; branchlets ferruginous-puberulent when young, glabrous and prominently lenticellate in age. Petioles ribbed, 2-7 cm long; rachis winged; petiole and rachis sparsely ferruginous-pubescent; leaflets in 2-5 pairs, obovate to elliptic, acute to acuminate, obtuse to rounded at base, densely tomentose to puberulent especially on midrib and veins below, the terminal pair 11-26 cm long, 4.5-12 cm wide. Spikes usually axillary in groups of 1-3; peduncles usually sparsely tomentose, 1-5(6) cm long; floral rachis much shorter, 0.5-2(3) cm long; bracts to 12 mm long; calyx and corolla sparsely sericeous; calyx 6-13 (17) mm long, the lobes to 2 mm long; corolla 18-30 mm long, the lobes to 3 mm long; stamens and styles 4-5.5 cm long. Legumes tetragonal with prominently ribbed corners, 11-30 cm long, 1.5-3.5 cm wide, ca 1.5 cm thick, glabrate to densely pubescent. Common, at least along the shore. Seasonal behavior uncertain. Flowers from August to May, especially from November to February. Most fruits mature in the rainy season. An extremely variable species. Often planted for shade in coffee plantations. Mexico to Panama; West Indies. In Panama, known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Bocas del Toro, San Bias, Code, Panama, and Darien and from premontane wet forest in Chiriqui (San Felix).

Tree, 7-15 m, the stems cylindrical or slightly angled, diminutively puberulent to glabrescent, without or with few and tiny lenticels. Leaves with petiole 4-8(-9.5) cm; petiolules 0.2-0.8 cm; leaflets 5-9, 4-12.5(-16.5) X 2.5-5 cm, elliptical to elliptical-obovate or eblascoid, obtuse to (more frequently) acute or cuneate to tapered at the base, obtuse to (more frequently) acuminate at the apex, entire or crenate to crenate-dentate (in the distal quarter), glabrous on both sides (except diminutively and inconspicuously puberulent on the midrib on the adaxial side and the nerves on the abaxial side). Inflorescences [subterminal or axillary], paniculate, up to at least 18.5 cm (-30 cm in fruit), the rachis densely tomentose; bracts ca. 1-2 mm (2.5 mm in fruit). Flowers with pedicel ca. 1 mm (—ca. 4 mm in fruit); sepals 1.5-2 mm (-2.5 mm in fruit), puberulent externally; petals greenish white, subequal or slightly longer than the sepals, villous (especially adaxially), densely villous-fringed; stamens with the filament ca. 2.5 mm, densely villous in the proximal half. Fruits 1.5-2 X 1-1.7 cm, obovoid, trilobulate (with each lobe subacute to rounded dorsally), densely tomentose, without lenticels when mature, with stipe 2-6 mm. Very humid forest, 50-150 m; [North vertical Caribbean slope], San Carlos Plain (Boca Tapada; Sardinales Hills). Flowers [in the months of] jul. [found in] S. Mexico, Belize, and Guatemala, Nicaragua—Bolivia and Venezuela, [Guyanas], Brazil. (Hammel 4: Trainer 13125, DUKE, MO; Zamora 6510, CR, INB, MO) Cupania scrobiculata is recognized by its entire leaflets or distally crenate to crenate-dentate, relatively large [inflorescences] and trilobulated [fruits], densely tomentose.

Tree or shrub, to 20 m; trunk to 23 cm dbh; outer bark thin, fissured, weakly flaky; inner bark reddish-brown, granular; wood light brown, hard, heavy; youngest stems pubescent; sap inconspicuous. Petioles to 5 mm long, moderately pubescent; stipules paired, subulate, to 5 mm long, subpersistent; blades elliptic-oblong, acuminate at apex, acute to rounded or subcordate at base, 4-12(14.5) cm long, 1.5-5 cm wide, glabrous above except on midrib, sparsely pubescent below, the trichomes denser on veins. Flowers in terminal racemose panicles to 8 cm long; rachis, branches, and pedicels tomentulose; pedicels slender, 2-3 mm long (appearing longer since flowers are often solitary at apices of branches); bracts and bracteoles narrowly lanceolate, 1-3.5 mm long, pubescent, lacking glands; calyx lobes 5, ovate, 3-4 mm long, rounded at apex, reflexed at anthesis, puberulent on both sides; petals 5, broadly elliptic, ca 5 mm long, rounded at both ends, white; stamens 3, long-exserted, arising from side of flower; filaments purplish above, 1-2 cm long, fused into a low ring arising from rim of hypanthium (remnants of a 4th and a 5th stamen persisting as sharp lobes on this ring); style ± equaling stamens and opposite them at anthesis, pilose and white below middle, purple above; ovary pilose-tomentose; stigma small, capitate. Drupes ovoid-oblong to rounded, ca 2.3 cm long, densely shortpubescent; exocarp thin, brownish-purple; mesocarp fleshy, sweet, tasty; seed ± ovate, ca 1.7 cm long, with irregular longitudinal grooves, abruptly narrowed at base. Common in the forest, mostly in the old forest. Flowers sporadically throughout the year, principally from November to May. Individual plants flower more than once a year, possibly as many as three times. The fruits mature throughout the year; white-faced monkeys eat the fruits in June and July.

Tree, 7-15 m, the stems cylindrical or slightly angled, diminutively puberulent to glabrescent, without or with few and tiny lenticels. Leaves with petiole 4-8(-9.5) cm; petiolules 0.2-0.8 cm; leaflets 5-9, 4-12.5(-16.5) X 2.5-5 cm, elliptical to elliptical-obovate or eblascoid, obtuse to (more frequently) acute or cuneate to tapered at the base, obtuse to (more frequently) acuminate at the apex, entire or crenate to crenate-dentate (in the distal quarter), glabrous on both sides (except diminutively and inconspicuously puberulent on the midrib on the adaxial side and the nerves on the abaxial side). Inflorescence subterminal or axillary, paniculate, up to at least 18.5 cm (-30 cm in fruit), the rachis densely tomentose; bracts ca. 1-2 mm (2.5 mm in fruit). Flowers with pedicel ca. 1 mm (—ca. 4 mm in fruit); sepals 1.5-2 mm (-2.5 mm in fruit), puberulent externally; petals greenish white, subequal or slightly longer than the sepals, villous (especially adaxially), densely villous-fringed; stamens with the filament ca. 2.5 mm, densely villous in the proximal half. Fruits 1.5-2 X 1-1.7 cm, obovoid, trilobulate (with each lobe subacute to rounded dorsally), densely tomentose, without lenticels when mature, with stipe 2-6 mm. Very humid forest, 50-150 m; northern vertical Caribbean region, San Carlos Plain (Boca Tapada; Sardinales Hills). Flowering months are July. Southern Mexico, Belize, and Guatemala, Nicaragua. Bolivia and Venezuela, Guayanas, Brazil. Cupania scrobiculata is recognized by its entire leaflets or distally crenate to crenate-dentate, relatively large inflorescences and trilobulated fruits, densely tomentose. Although Cupania scrobiculata was not confirmed for Costa Rica until very recently (with material in fruit) and is known from the country by only two samples, Cupania scrobiculata is very abundant in the surroundings of Boca Tapada.

Dioecious shrub or tree, to 15 m tall; trunk slender or to 20 cm dbh and deeply invaginated; stems sericeous when very young, glabrate in age, with conspicuous leaf scars. Leaves somewhat clustered at apex of branchlets; stipules caducous, to 1 cm long, sericeous, leaving a conspicuous interpetiolar line of trichomes; petioles 6-14 mm long, sericeous to glabrate; blades ovate-elliptic to obovate-elliptic, abruptly short-acuminate, usually obtuse and ± decurrent onto petiole at base, 7-13(21) cm long, 3.5-8 (12) cm wide, glabrous or with sparse long trichomes on major veins below and tufts of trichomes in axils, the margins ciliate and ± revolute.

Trees, climbing shrubs, or lianas; stipules absent. Leaves compound, odd-pinnate or trifoliate, indumentum of simple trichomes, the blade sometimes with glandular dots on the underside, margin entire; petiole and petiolules pulvinated. Inflorescences in panicles, racemes, or spike-like, axillary or terminal. Flowers bisexual, white, yellowish, or pale pink; sepals 5, valvate or imbricate; petals 5, free; stamens 10, forming a short tube at the base; ovary superior, carpels 1-5, style one per carpel; ovules 2 per carpel. Fruit in follicles, often red; seeds 1 per fruit, black, the aril bright red, yellow, white, or orange.
The family consists of 16 genera and about 300–350 species, pantropical, with a distribution center in western Africa; for tropical America, 5 genera and 108 species are known; 3 genera and 9 species in CR.
It is characterized by its compound leaves, mainly trifoliate or odd-pinnate, leaflets alternate on the rachis, sometimes with dendritic trichomes, petioles clearly pulvinated, stipules absent, and the fruit follicles with a black seed with a reddish basal aril. In vegetative form, its general appearance relates it directly to the family Fabaceae, but several of the characteristics mentioned earlier allow it to be separated.
Traditionally, the family has been placed within the Order Rosales, or in close relation to the Order Sapindales, and some have suggested a link between such Orders. However, recent molecular studies suggest that its placement is in the Order Oxalidales, along with families such as: Oxalidaceae, Cunnoniaceae, Elaeocarpaceae, etc.
